title: Inheriting Property Without a Will: Who Inherits, How Is It Divided?
desc: When parents die without a will, how is the house and land divided? Lines of heirs, substitute inheritance, the 30-year limitation period, division document.
summary: When the deceased leaves no will, property is divided by the lines of heirs in the 2015 Civil Code; this article explains who inherits, how it is divided and the limitation periods to remember.
body: p

Many families worry about dividing the house and land when a parent has died without leaving a will. In that case the estate is divided by law, that is, by the lines of heirs, conditions and order set out in the 2015 Civil Code.
h2
1. When is property divided by law?
p
Under Article 650 of the Civil Code, statutory succession applies when:
ul
There is no will, or the will is not valid;
The heirs named in the will die before, or at the same time as, the testator;
A person designated in the will has no right to inherit or refuses to accept the estate.
p
The part of the house and land not mentioned in the will, or relating to a part of the will that is not effective, is also divided by law.
h2
2. What does the estate include?
p

The estate includes the deceased's separate property and the deceased's share of property co-owned with others (Article 612). For example, if a house is the joint property of a husband and wife and the husband dies, only the husband's share of the house is part of the estate; the wife's share still belongs to the wife.
h2
3. The three lines of heirs
p
Under Article 651:
ul
First line: the deceased's spouse, biological father and mother, adoptive father and mother, biological children and adopted children.
Second line: the deceased's paternal and maternal grandparents, full brothers and sisters, and full grandchildren where the deceased is the grandparent.

Third line: great-grandparents; full paternal and maternal uncles and aunts; full nephews and nieces where the deceased is the uncle or aunt; full great-grandchildren where the deceased is the great-grandparent.
p

Persons in the same line share equally. A later line inherits only when no one remains in the earlier line (because they have died, have no right to inherit, have been disinherited or have refused the estate).
p

Adopted children and adoptive parents inherit from each other (Article 653). Stepchildren and stepfathers or stepmothers inherit from each other if they cared for and raised each other like father and child or mother and child (Article 654).
h2
4. Substitute inheritance: a child who died before the parent
p

If a child of the person leaving the estate dies before or at the same time as that person, the grandchild receives the share the grandchild's parent would have received if alive; if the grandchild has also died, the great-grandchild receives it (Article 652).
p

Example: Mr A dies without a will, leaving a house as his separate property. In the first line there remain Mr A's wife and two children B and C; child D died earlier, leaving one child E. The house is divided into 4 equal shares for the wife, B, C and D; D's share is taken by E through substitute inheritance.
h2
5. Who may not inherit?
p

Under Article 621, the following may not inherit: a person convicted of intentionally infringing on the life or health of, or seriously mistreating or tormenting, the person leaving the estate; a person who seriously breached the duty to support the person leaving the estate; a person who deceived or coerced in making the will, or forged, altered, destroyed or concealed the will, and similar acts - unless the person leaving the estate knew and still allowed them to inherit under the will.
p
An heir has the right to refuse the estate; the refusal must be in writing and made before the estate is divided; it may not be made to avoid property obligations owed to others (Article 620).
h2
6. Steps for dividing the house and land, and time limits
ol
The heirs meet and agree on appointing a manager, the person who divides the estate, and the way of dividing; every agreement must be in writing (Article 656).
Settle the deceased's obligations in priority order: funeral costs, outstanding maintenance payments, costs of preserving the estate, and so on (Article 658).

Divide the estate; it may be divided in kind, and if it cannot be divided equally, the heirs agree on a valuation and on who takes the item; if they cannot agree, it is sold and the proceeds divided (Clause 2, Article 660).

Notarise the estate division document: the dossier additionally needs the death certificate, papers proving the relationship to the person leaving the estate, and the house and land papers (Article 59 of the 2024 Notarisation Law; Point c, Clause 3, Article 27 of the Land Law).
Carry out the change registration procedure to transfer the house and land to the recipient's name.
p

The limitation period for requesting division of an estate that is real estate is 30 years from the time succession opens (the date the property owner dies); for requesting confirmation or rejection of an inheritance right it is 10 years; for requesting heirs to perform the deceased's property obligations it is 3 years (Article 623; Article 611).
p
Inheritance between parents, children, full siblings and similar relatives is exempt from personal income tax; see Taxes on gifting and inheriting property.
note

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace the legal texts. The 2024 Notarisation Law has been amended (Law 106/2025/QH15 - not yet in our library; Law 04/2026/QH16 takes effect on 1 January 2027). The 2024 Land Law is partly expired. Where there is a dispute over dividing the estate, ask a notarial practice organisation or a lawyer.
